sentences: She found artificial intelligence transforming her industry faster than anyone had predicted.
He found AI tools becoming standard in Australian workplaces across professional services.
Artificial intelligence is the simulation of human intelligence by computer systems.
She found AI applications in Australian healthcare, legal services, agriculture, and manufacturing.
He found the Australian government developing an AI Ethics Framework to guide responsible deployment.
Artificial intelligence raises issues of bias, transparency, accountability, and workforce displacement.
She found AI-generated content requiring the same critical evaluation as any other source.
He found Australian universities adapting academic integrity policies to address AI-assisted work.
Artificial intelligence in Australia is subject to the Privacy Act and developing sector-specific regulation.
She describes artificial intelligence as the technology that most changed what she considered uniquely human about her work.
She found the Optus and Medibank data breaches making data privacy a mainstream Australian concern.
He found data privacy governed by the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles.
Data privacy is the right of individuals to control how their personal information is collected and used.
She found the Privacy Act applying to organisations with annual turnover above three million dollars.
He found data privacy reform underway — the Privacy Act under review for the digital age.
Data privacy protections in Australia include rights to access, correction, and complaint.
She found data privacy most directly tested by large-scale breaches exposing millions of Australians.
He found the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requiring organisations to report significant breaches to the OAIC.
Data privacy and digital identity are among the most consequential policy areas of the decade.
She describes data privacy as the digital right she most wanted enforced by law — not just trusted to corporate goodwill.
She joined a startup in her second year in Australia — it was the most demanding and educational environment she had worked in.
He found the Australian startup ecosystem centred in Sydney and Melbourne — but growing in Brisbane and Perth.
A startup is a young company designed to scale rapidly, typically technology-based.
She found Australian startups including Atlassian, Canva, and Afterpay achieving global scale.
He found startup culture emphasising speed, iteration, and tolerance for failure.
Startups in Australia access capital through angel investors, venture capital, and government grants.
She found Atlassian — founded in Sydney — among the most successful technology startups in Australian history.
He found the startup community supported through accelerators like Startmate and SBE Australia.
Startups disrupt established industries — fintech challenging banks, proptech changing real estate.
She describes working in a startup as the career experience that most required her to be comfortable with uncertainty.
She led the digital transformation project — moving her organisation from paper to cloud systems.
He found digital transformation the dominant business agenda item across Australian industries.
Digital transformation is the process of integrating digital technology into all areas of a business.
She found digital transformation in Australian government accelerated by the COVID period.
He found the Digital Transformation Agency — DTA — coordinating federal government digitisation.
Digital transformation requires cultural change as much as technology adoption.
She found digital transformation creating new roles — and displacing others — across Australian workplaces.
He found the myGov platform the most visible expression of government digital transformation.
Digital transformation in healthcare produced telehealth, digital prescriptions, and MyHealth Record.
She describes digital transformation as the change she most had to lead through rather than simply observe.
She found automation changing the nature of her team's work — routine tasks disappeared, complex ones grew.
He found automation the technology trend most directly affecting employment in Australian manufacturing and logistics.
Automation is the use of technology to perform tasks with reduced human intervention.
She found automation in Australian agriculture — robotic fruit picking and precision irrigation — significant.
He found automation anxiety real among Australian workers — but its pace and scope contested.
Automation tends to displace routine tasks while creating demand for higher-order skills.
She found the Future of Work discussion in Australia centering on automation, retraining, and social support.
He found automation in customer service — chatbots, self-service kiosks — the most visible change.
Automation creates productivity gains — the policy question is how those gains are distributed.
She describes automation as the technological force she most needed to understand to give her children useful career advice.
She migrated her business to cloud computing — she accessed everything from any device.
He found cloud computing adoption in Australian business nearly universal among professional services.
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services — storage, software, processing — over the internet.
She found cloud providers including AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud operating Australian data centres.
He found cloud computing enabling remote work infrastructure — the pandemic accelerated adoption.
Cloud computing raises data sovereignty questions — where is the data stored and who can access it.
She found the Australian government's Secure Cloud Strategy guiding agency cloud adoption.
He found cloud computing reducing IT infrastructure costs significantly for small businesses.
Cloud computing requires robust internet — she found regional Australia's limited connectivity a real barrier.
She describes cloud computing as the technology shift that most changed how she thought about where her work lived.
She enabled two-factor authentication on all financial accounts after hearing about a friend's bank fraud.
He found two-factor authentication the single most effective security measure he could take.
Two-factor authentication — 2FA — requires both a password and a second verification to access an account.
She found 2FA via SMS, authenticator app, or hardware key — she preferred the authenticator app.
He found 2FA now the standard for banking, government, and email in Australia.
Two-factor authentication significantly reduces the risk of account takeover — even if the password is stolen.
She found myGov, the ATO, and banking apps all supporting 2FA.
He found passkeys emerging as the next step beyond 2FA — she researched them carefully.
Two-factor authentication adds seconds to login and enormously reduces risk — the trade-off was obvious.
She describes enabling two-factor authentication as the ten-minute task that most changed her digital security posture.
She found her details in the Optus data breach — she changed every password immediately.
He found data breaches becoming Australia's most consequential consumer security events.
A data breach is a security incident where protected information is accessed or disclosed without authorisation.
She found the Optus and Medibank breaches in 2022 exposing millions of Australians' personal data.
He found data breach notification to affected individuals required under Australian law.
Data breaches in Australia must be reported to the OAIC — the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.
She found the ACSC — Australian Cyber Security Centre — providing guidance after major breaches.
He found the ID Support service helping Australians replace government documents after a data breach.
Data breaches cause financial loss, identity theft risk, and lasting reputational damage.
She describes the data breach notification email as the message she most dreaded receiving — and most needed to act on immediately.
She switched to a fintech bank — the app-based service and fee-free international transfers suited her lifestyle.
He found Australian fintech producing some of the most successful financial technology globally.
Fintech is the use of technology to deliver financial services — including payments, lending, and insurance.
She found Australian fintechs including Afterpay, Zip, and Up Bank reshaping consumer finance.
He found fintech innovation in payments, lending, wealth management, and remittances.
Fintech companies in Australia are regulated by ASIC and APRA depending on the service provided.
She found the fintech banking experience frictionless — accounts opened in minutes, no branch required.
He found the fintech sector the most globally competitive area of Australian technology.
Fintechs have challenged traditional banks on fee transparency, user experience, and product innovation.
She describes adopting a fintech bank as the financial decision that most improved her daily banking experience.
She pays with her digital wallet at almost every transaction — she has not carried cash in months.
He found Apple Pay and Google Pay the dominant digital wallet platforms in Australia.
A digital wallet is a software application that stores payment card information for contactless transactions.
She found digital wallets accepted at the vast majority of Australian retail and hospitality venues.
He found digital wallet transactions processed through the same contactless terminal as physical cards.
Digital wallets in Australia are subject to the same fraud protections as physical card payments.
She found her digital wallet storing multiple cards — debit, credit, and loyalty cards in one place.
He found digital wallets eliminating the risk of card skimming — the card number is not transmitted.
Digital wallets also store boarding passes, tickets, and ID — she found the integration practical.
She describes the digital wallet as the technology adoption that most quietly eliminated a physical object she used to always carry.
She negotiated remote work for three days per week — she found her productivity higher at home.
He found remote work permanently reshaping the Australian office sector.
Remote work is employment conducted from a location other than the employer's office — typically home.
She found remote work policy the most debated HR issue in Australian workplaces post-pandemic.
He found remote work enabling regional living — he moved to Daylesford and kept his Melbourne salary.
Remote work requires reliable internet, suitable workspace, and digital collaboration tools.
She found Fair Work addressing remote work requests — employees now have the right to request flexible arrangements.
He found remote work culture varying enormously by organisation — some embracing it, others resisting.
Remote work has contributed to regional property price growth — urban professionals relocating.
She describes remote work as the employment arrangement that most changed her relationship with her city — she missed it less than expected.
She found video conferencing replacing most domestic travel — the environmental and cost savings were significant.
He found Zoom, Teams, and Google Meet the platforms that most defined Australian workplace collaboration.
Video conferencing is real-time audio and video communication between participants in different locations.
She found video conferencing etiquette — camera on, microphone muted when not speaking — an unwritten professional code.
He found video conferencing enabling her to work across international time zones from her home office.
Video conferencing fatigue — Zoom fatigue — became a recognised workplace wellbeing issue.
She found video conferencing quality dependent on broadband speed — her NBN connection mattered.
He found video conferencing most effective for small group discussion — large webinars worked differently.
Video conferencing has reduced the need for some office space — and reshaped the purpose of the office.
She describes video conferencing as the technology that most sustained her working relationships through the years she worked from home.
She found e-commerce growing in Australia faster than physical retail in every category she tracked.
He found Australian e-commerce reaching over sixty billion dollars annually.
E-commerce is the buying and selling of goods and services over the internet.
She found Australian e-commerce including both domestic retailers and international platforms like Amazon and ASOS.
He found the e-commerce logistics chain — warehousing, last-mile delivery, and returns — the most complex part.
E-commerce businesses in Australia must comply with the ACL regardless of digital channel.
She found e-commerce enabling small Australian businesses to reach national and international customers.
He found e-commerce platforms charging commissions that significantly affected seller margins.
E-commerce is reshaping retail property — vacancy in shopping centres rising as online shopping grows.
She describes e-commerce as the commercial shift she most felt as both a consumer and a small business owner.
She found the smart home devices the most convenient and the most privacy-concerning technology she owned.
He found smart home adoption in Australia growing most rapidly in lighting, security, and energy management.
A smart home uses internet-connected devices to automate and remotely control household functions.
She found smart thermostats, voice assistants, and security cameras the most adopted smart home technologies.
He found smart home devices raising legitimate privacy concerns — audio and video data collected.
Smart home integration through platforms like Google Home and Amazon Alexa enabled voice control.
She found smart home energy management — monitoring appliance consumption — her most practically valuable application.
He found smart home devices sometimes lacking interoperability — different brands not always compatible.
Smart homes can improve energy efficiency — she reduced her electricity bill using smart scheduling.
She describes the smart home as the technology adoption she most consistently underestimated both the benefits and the risks of.
She found the Australian digital identity framework streamlining access to multiple government services.
He found digital identity the infrastructure that most determined the convenience and security of online services.
Digital identity is the digital representation of an individual used to verify who they are online.
She found myGovID the Australian government's digital identity credential — linked to ATO, Centrelink, and Medicare.
He found digital identity enabling secure document upload without physical presence at an agency.
Digital identity systems require balancing convenience against privacy and security risk.
She found the Trusted Digital Identity Framework the policy architecture governing Australian digital ID.
He found digital identity becoming relevant for private sector services — banking, healthcare, and property.
Digital identity fraud is a significant and growing form of crime — protecting credentials was essential.
She describes digital identity as the infrastructure she most wanted to be governed by clear law before it governed her.
She reported the harmful content to the eSafety Commissioner — it was removed within hours.
He found the eSafety Commissioner Australia's world-leading online safety regulator.
eSafety is a term for the practices and protections ensuring safe and positive online experiences.
She found the eSafety Commissioner at esafety.gov.au providing resources for children, parents, and adults.
He found eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant the most prominent online safety advocate in Australia.
eSafety regulation in Australia includes industry codes, content removal powers, and legal obligations.
She found eSafety resources addressing cyberbullying, image-based abuse, and scams.
He found the Online Safety Act 2021 giving the eSafety Commissioner significant new powers.
eSafety education in Australian schools was growing — she found curriculum resources available.
She describes the eSafety Commissioner as the institution that most practically protected her family's online experience.
She found online safety education the most urgent digital literacy need for her children.
He found Australian parents consistently rating online safety among their top parenting concerns.
Online safety is the practice of protecting oneself and others from harm in digital environments.
She found online safety risks including cyberbullying, grooming, scams, and harmful content.
He found the Online Safety Act giving Australians the right to have harmful content removed.
Online safety in Australia is regulated by the eSafety Commissioner — with powers across major platforms.
She found online safety resources for different age groups at the Raising Children Network.
He found online safety conversations with his children requiring ongoing updating — the platforms changed.
Online safety requires both technical tools and human judgment — filters alone were insufficient.
She describes online safety as the parenting challenge she most consistently underestimated in its complexity.
She found agritech the most practically significant technology sector for regional Australia.
He found Australian agritech startups developing precision irrigation, drone monitoring, and livestock management.
Agritech is the application of technology to improve agricultural production and efficiency.
She found agritech enabling Australian farmers to reduce inputs while maintaining yield.
He found the CSIRO the most significant agritech research institution in Australia.
Agritech in Australia covers crop monitoring, automated harvesting, soil sensing, and supply chain tracking.
She found agritech investment growing as climate pressure and labour shortages drove technology adoption.
He found agritech companies supporting Australian farmers to compete globally despite high labour costs.
Agritech data collection raises ownership questions — who owned the data generated on a farm.
She describes agritech as the technology sector she most valued for its practical impact on people doing real work in real landscapes.

sentences: She found CSIRO Wi-Fi — yes, CSIRO helped develop wireless networking — the most surprising Australian tech fact.
He found the CSIRO the most significant scientific research institution in Australia.
CSIRO — Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation — is Australia's national science agency.
She found CSIRO conducting research across agriculture, health, environment, and materials science.
He found CSIRO's contribution to Wi-Fi technology one of Australia's most commercially significant inventions.
CSIRO employs around five thousand scientists and researchers across Australia.
She found CSIRO working in partnership with industry, universities, and government on applied science.
He found CSIRO's Data61 division the most prominent Australian artificial intelligence and data research unit.
CSIRO has contributed to body armour, polymer banknotes, and solar panels — among many others.
She describes CSIRO as the Australian institution she most wished was better known to the public it served.
She found the innovation hub in Pyrmont housing dozens of technology startups — the energy was tangible.
He found innovation hubs the physical infrastructure of Australia's startup ecosystem.
An innovation hub is a co-working and networking environment designed to support startups and entrepreneurs.
She found Stone and Chalk — a fintech hub in Sydney — among Australia's most prominent.
He found innovation hubs often co-located with universities — enabling research commercialisation.
Innovation hubs provide mentorship, networks, office space, and investor access.
She found innovation hubs in Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide, and Canberra alongside the major eastern cities.
He found innovation hub programs funded by government, corporates, and universities.
Innovation hubs produce collaboration between established companies and emerging startups.
She describes the innovation hub as the workspace that most made her feel the future of Australian business was being built in real time.
She tracks her sleep, steps, and heart rate with a wearable — her GP found the data useful.
He found wearable technology adoption in Australia growing most rapidly in health and fitness.
Wearable technology is electronic devices worn on the body — smart watches, fitness trackers, health monitors.
She found smart watches providing health metrics that supported early detection of health issues.
He found wearable technology raising privacy questions — health data collected at every moment.
Wearable technology data is increasingly used by health insurers — with privacy implications.
She found the Apple Watch, Fitbit, and Garmin the most common wearables in Australian workplaces.
He found wearable technology in industrial settings monitoring worker fatigue and safety.
Wearables produce continuous health data — the aggregation was powerful and the implications significant.
She describes her wearable as the technology that most consistently helped her understand her own body.
She found blockchain technology moving beyond cryptocurrency into supply chain, property, and health records.
He found blockchain the most discussed and least understood technology concept in Australian business.
Blockchain is a distributed digital ledger recording transactions across many computers — immutable and transparent.
She found Australian blockchain applications in agricultural provenance — tracking beef from farm to consumer.
He found the ASX exploring blockchain for equity settlement — a significant infrastructure project.
Blockchain enables trustless transactions — no central authority required to verify the exchange.
She found blockchain-based property title systems piloted in some Australian jurisdictions.
He found the energy sector exploring blockchain for peer-to-peer energy trading — rooftop solar.
Blockchain's environmental cost — energy-intensive proof-of-work systems — was a legitimate concern.
She describes blockchain as the technology she most needed to look past the hype to understand the practical application.
She uses a VPN when working on public Wi-Fi — the security benefit was clear.
He found VPN usage in Australia growing among privacy-conscious workers and remote employees.
A VPN — Virtual Private Network — encrypts internet traffic and masks the user's IP address.
She found VPNs commonly used by Australians working remotely to access corporate systems securely.
He found VPN use enabling Australians to access geo-restricted streaming content from overseas libraries.
VPNs in Australia are legal — some countries restrict their use, but Australia does not.
She found corporate VPNs standard in Australian workplaces for remote access to secure systems.
He found consumer VPN providers varying in quality and privacy policy — she researched before subscribing.
VPNs add a layer of security but do not guarantee complete anonymity.
She describes the VPN as the digital tool she most wished she had understood and adopted earlier.
She found proptech platforms like realestate.com.au and Domain transforming how Australians buy and rent.
He found Australian proptech producing significant innovation in rental, sales, and property management.
Proptech is the application of technology to the property industry — buying, selling, renting, and managing.
She found proptech enabling virtual property inspections — useful when relocating interstate.
He found proptech producing data transparency that had not previously been available to buyers.
Proptech startups in Australia include platforms for rent payments, maintenance requests, and tenant screening.
She found proptech helping landlords manage properties remotely — lease, payments, and communication digitised.
He found PEXA — the electronic property settlement platform — the most significant proptech infrastructure in Australia.
Proptech is reshaping traditional real estate agencies — some functions automated, others enhanced.
She describes proptech as the technology sector that most directly changed the experience of finding and managing her home.
She found the digital divide affecting older Australians, low-income households, and remote communities.
He found the digital divide the most significant barrier to equal participation in Australian digital services.
The digital divide is the gap between those with access to digital technology and those without.
She found the digital divide worsened by slow or unreliable internet in regional and remote Australia.
He found public libraries providing the most accessible digital access point for disadvantaged communities.
The digital divide in Australia is addressed through programs like the School Connect and Family Access Network.
She found digital skills training targeting older Australians a significant social inclusion initiative.
He found the digital divide intersecting with income, age, disability, and geographic remoteness.
The digital divide becomes critical when government services are delivered primarily online.
She describes the digital divide as the inequality she most wanted addressed before more services went exclusively digital.
She designs all her social media content in Canva — it is the most accessible design tool she has used.
He found Canva one of Australia's most successful technology companies — valued at over thirty billion dollars.
Canva is an Australian online design platform enabling users to create graphics, presentations, and documents.
She found Canva founded in Perth in 2013 by Melanie Perkins — among Australia's most celebrated founders.
He found Canva used by over one hundred million people globally — a unicorn and beyond.
Canva is headquartered in Sydney and employs thousands of staff across multiple global offices.
She found Canva's free tier sufficient for most of her design needs.
He found Canva representing the kind of Australian software company that proved the country could compete globally.
Canva expanded beyond design into document creation, whiteboards, and video tools.
She describes Canva as the Australian technology product she most regularly used and most frequently recommended.
She found Atlassian — JIRA, Confluence, Trello — the tools that ran most Australian tech workplaces.
He found Atlassian among Australia's greatest technology success stories.
Atlassian is an Australian technology company producing software development and collaboration tools.
She found Atlassian founded in Sydney in 2002 by Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar.
He found JIRA the most widely used project management tool in Australian software development.
Atlassian listed on the NASDAQ in 2015 — one of Australia's most significant technology milestones.
She found Atlassian's founders among Australia's most prominent technology philanthropists.
He found Atlassian's commitment to a remote-friendly workforce ahead of the broader industry.
Atlassian's success demonstrated that world-class software companies could be built in Australia.
She describes Atlassian as the Australian company that most changed her professional tool kit and her idea of what Australian technology could achieve.
She found the internet of things connecting her home appliances — the fridge tracked what she needed.
He found IoT devices in Australian agriculture, utilities, and healthcare growing rapidly.
The internet of things — IoT — is the network of physical devices connected to the internet and sharing data.
She found IoT applications in smart meters, remote monitoring of water pumps, and precision agriculture.
He found IoT security a significant vulnerability — many devices shipped with poor default settings.
The internet of things is generating data at scales that require AI and cloud computing to analyse.
She found Australian water authorities using IoT sensors to detect leaks and monitor usage.
He found the IoT most visible in consumer products — smart speakers, connected TVs, and appliances.
IoT raises environmental concerns — millions of short-lived devices contributing to e-waste.
She describes the internet of things as the technology trend she most needed to understand before it became embedded in everything she could not see.
She found digital literacy the most consistently underfunded workforce skill in Australian organisations.
He found digital literacy gaps the most common barrier to organisational digital transformation.
Digital literacy is the ability to use digital technology effectively, critically, and safely.
She found digital literacy encompassing basic computing, online safety, information evaluation, and communication.
He found the Australian Digital Inclusion Index measuring digital literacy and access across the population.
Digital literacy differs from technical expertise — it is a baseline skill, not a specialisation.
She found digital literacy training the most valued professional development she had received in the past year.
He found digital literacy gaps widest among older workers and those in manual occupations.
Digital literacy is increasingly essential for citizenship — services, communication, and information now digital.
She describes digital literacy as the foundational capability she most believed every Australian deserved to be taught.
She found the government website's poor user experience the most frustrating digital encounter of her week.
He found user experience design the professional discipline that most shaped the digital services he relied on.
User experience — UX — is the overall experience a person has when interacting with a product or system.
She found good user experience invisible — she only noticed when it was absent.
He found UX design a growing profession in Australian technology and government services.
User experience encompasses usability, accessibility, and emotional response to digital interfaces.
She found Australian government digital services improving in user experience — but unevenly.
He found UX research — observing how real users interacted with a product — the most honest form of feedback.
User experience underpins adoption — the best-designed service went unused if the experience was poor.
She describes great user experience as the design quality she most took for granted until she used something without it.
She worked as a digital nomad for a year — co-working spaces from Bali to Byron Bay.
He found the digital nomad lifestyle both liberating and socially isolating.
A digital nomad is a person who works remotely while travelling — typically using laptops and digital tools.
She found digital nomad communities forming in Australian regional towns with good internet and affordable living.
He found Byron Bay and Noosa developing significant digital nomad populations.
Digital nomads contribute to the economies of the places they reside temporarily.
She found digital nomadism raising questions about tax residency, home, and belonging.
He found co-working spaces the essential infrastructure for the digital nomad lifestyle.
Digital nomads often work in creative, consulting, and technology roles — location-independent outputs.
She describes the digital nomad year as the working arrangement she most learned from — and most wanted to leave behind.
She found cybersecurity the most underprepared area in most Australian businesses she had advised.
He found the Australian Cyber Security Centre — ACSC — the primary government resource for organisations.
Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems, networks, and programs from digital attacks.
She found Australia's Cyber Security Strategy 2023-2030 setting ambitious goals for national cyber resilience.
He found cybersecurity certification — Essential Eight — the standard framework for Australian businesses.
Cybersecurity threats include ransomware, phishing, data theft, and infrastructure attacks.
She found the ACSC offering free cybersecurity advice for small and medium businesses.
He found cybersecurity professionals among the most in-demand workers in the Australian technology sector.
Cybersecurity breaches in Australia have affected hospitals, universities, and critical infrastructure.
She describes cybersecurity as the risk management discipline she most wanted every Australian organisation to take seriously before the incident — not after.
She found data.gov.au hosting thousands of Australian government datasets freely available.
He found open data enabling researchers, journalists, and developers to build useful tools.
Open data is government or institutional information made freely available for public use.
She found Australian open data spanning health statistics, transport networks, and environmental monitoring.
He found open data driving transparency — budget expenditure, tender awards, and regulatory decisions.
Open data publication is a commitment of modern democratic government — she evaluated parties on it.
She found open data used by startups building apps on public transport timetables and health facility locations.
He found the quality of open data varying — some datasets poorly maintained or inadequately documented.
Open data enables accountability — she used it in the advocacy campaign she ran.
She describes open data as the government resource that most empowered citizens who knew it existed.
She found the platform economy reshaping how work was organised in Australia — delivery, care, and transport.
He found platform economy workers the most debated category in Australian labour law reform.
The platform economy is an economic system where digital platforms mediate exchanges between producers and consumers.
She found Uber, Airbnb, Airtasker, and Care.com among the most significant platforms in Australia.
He found platform economy workers often classified as contractors — denied employee protections.
The platform economy creates flexibility but often at the cost of employment rights and income security.
She found Fair Work extending protections to some gig economy workers through new legislative frameworks.
He found the platform economy enabling her to earn income flexibly between career stages.
Platform economies have disrupted taxis, hotels, media, and retail — benefiting consumers and pressuring incumbents.
She describes the platform economy as the labour market shift she most needed to understand both as a worker and as a consumer.
She drove for a rideshare platform for six months — the gig economy filled the income gap between jobs.
He found the gig economy offering flexibility that traditional employment could not.
The gig economy is a labour market characterised by short-term contracts, freelance work, and task-based engagements.
She found gig economy workers in Australia encompassing ride-hailing, food delivery, and professional services.
He found gig economy income variable — a good week could be twice a poor one.
Gig economy workers in Australia lacked paid leave, superannuation contributions from platforms, and redundancy entitlements.
She found Fair Work reforms in 2023 providing minimum standards for some gig economy workers.
He found the gig economy most valuable as a transitional arrangement — not a permanent career.
Gig economy platforms are now required to contribute superannuation for workers above certain earnings.
She describes the gig economy as the work arrangement that most clearly showed the trade-off between freedom and security.
